title: The history of concept art
tagline: 120 years from a magician drawing his own moon sets to whole worlds painted on tablets before a single frame is shot.
intro: Before a film is made, someone has to imagine how it will look. At first directors and set designers sketched it themselves. In the 1930s Disney hired illustrators just to paint ideas that would inspire everyone else, and the job we now call concept art grew from there. Paintings helped sell films, then digital brushes made ideas faster to try, and today big art departments design whole worlds, from Hollywood to Hyderabad.

eras.name: Set sketches and silent spectacle
eras.summary: Filmmakers and set designers draw and build their own worlds. There is no separate job yet for painting ideas.

eras.name: The inspirational sketch
eras.summary: Disney hires illustrators to paint moods and places that inspire the animators, and Hollywood invents the production designer.

eras.name: The concept painter
eras.summary: Paintings and key drawings plan creatures, spaceships and cities, and help directors sell whole films to studios.

eras.name: Digital brushes
eras.summary: Pressure pens, Photoshop, Painter and 3D sculpting let artists try ideas quickly and change them without starting again.

eras.name: Worldbuilding at scale
eras.summary: Large art departments design entire kingdoms and styles, on tablets as well as paper, in India and around the world.

events.title: A magician designs his own moon
events.text: Méliès wrote, directed and helped design A Trip to the Moon. He sculpted prototypes for the moon creatures' heads and feet himself, and drew sketches for the film's poster. Historians think he also worked with a painter on the painted scenery.
events.why: It showed that a film's look could be invented on paper and in the workshop before the camera rolled.

events.title: A city of the future, designed first
events.who: Otto Hunte, Erich Kettelhut and Karl Vollbrecht
events.text: Fritz Lang's Metropolis needed a whole future city. Three art directors designed it, mixing modern, art deco and Gothic ideas. The look was partly inspired by Lang's visit to New York.
events.why: It proved that designers could build a believable world that did not exist yet.

events.title: The first Oscar for art direction
events.text: Menzies, a trained illustrator, won the very first Academy Award for art direction for The Dove and The Tempest. He planned how films should look with his own drawings.
events.why: Designing a film's look was now recognised as a craft of its own.

events.title: Disney's first inspirational sketch artist
events.text: Swiss-born Albert Hurter joined Disney and spent about ten years drawing whatever he liked: odd creatures, cottages, trees and moods. The animators used his sketches as a starting point. He is widely described as Disney's first inspirational sketch artist.
events.why: It created a job whose only purpose was to spark ideas for everyone else.

events.title: The words "concept art" appear
events.text: The term concept art is often said to come from Disney, which used it as early as the 1930s. At the studio, artists painted ideas for scenes long before animation began. Many different ideas were tried before one was chosen.
events.why: It gave a name to a stage of filmmaking that is now in almost every big film and game.

events.title: A storybook look for Snow White and Pinocchio
events.text: Tenggren, a Swedish book illustrator, worked at Disney from 1936 to 1939. His paintings of forests, cottages and villages helped set the European fairy-tale look of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) and Pinocchio (1940). Layout artists used them as guides.
events.why: A few paintings could steer the look of a whole film made by hundreds of people.

events.title: The first "production designer"
events.text: Producer David O. Selznick gave Menzies a new title for Gone with the Wind: production designer. It meant he had the final word on how the whole film looked. He won a special Oscar for using colour to set the mood.
events.why: The job of designing a film's whole look before filming now had a name and a credit.

events.title: Dark mountains and a little mermaid
events.text: Danish illustrator Kay Nielsen worked at Disney from 1937 to 1941. His art was used for the Night on Bald Mountain and Ave Maria part of Fantasia (1940). He also painted ideas for a Little Mermaid film that was only made in 1989.
events.why: Concept art can wait for decades and still shape a film.

events.title: A future director learns design
events.text: Ray started work at the advertising agency D.J. Keymer as a junior visualiser. He also illustrated a children's edition of the novel Pather Panchali. That book later became his first film.
events.why: His training as a commercial artist shaped how he planned films in pictures.

events.title: Mary Blair's bold colours
events.text: Blair joined Disney in 1940 as a colour stylist and travelled to Latin America with Walt Disney in 1941. Her concept art set the style of Cinderella (1950), Alice in Wonderland (1951) and Peter Pan (1953). She used bright, unexpected colours in strong contrast.
events.why: She showed that colour choices in concept art could give a film its whole feeling.

events.title: A film planned in a sketchbook
events.text: Ray had no written script for Pather Panchali at first. He drew its scenes in pen, brush and ink in a sketchbook, and showed these pictures to people he hoped would fund the film. It came out in 1955 and won prizes around the world.
events.why: A sequence of simple drawings was enough to plan, and to sell, a masterpiece.

events.title: Key drawings for stop-motion monsters
events.text: Before animating his models, Harryhausen made dramatic key drawings of the big moments, such as a sailor fighting a skeleton in 1957. These plans led to the famous skeleton battle in Jason and the Argonauts (1963). His foundation now cares for an archive of more than 50,000 items.
events.why: One strong drawing of a key moment can guide months of frame-by-frame work.

events.title: A ride that looks like a painting
events.text: Walt Disney asked Blair to help design the It's a Small World ride for the 1964 New York World's Fair. The finished ride closely follows her style. It was later rebuilt in Disney parks around the world.
events.why: Concept art could shape real places people walk through, not only films.

events.title: The red notebook
events.text: Ray kept a red cloth notebook, a kheror khata, for each film. It held notes, sketches, music and storyboards. The one for Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne (1969) has been digitised with its sketchbook for anyone to explore.
events.why: It shows one artist planning a whole fantasy film by hand, page by page.

events.title: Paintings that sold Star Wars
events.text: Lucas asked McQuarrie to paint several scenes from his Star Wars script. Lucas took the paintings to 20th Century Fox, and they helped convince the studio to fund the film. McQuarrie also designed many of its characters and sets.
events.why: It made the concept painting famous as a tool for selling an idea, not just planning it.

events.title: A "visual futurist" designs two films at once
events.text: Mead, a former industrial designer, was the first person hired for Blade Runner. He started with vehicles and ended up designing streets, buildings and props. At the same time he designed for Tron, and he invented the screen credit visual futurist.
events.why: It showed how one concept designer could shape a whole imagined future.

events.title: The pen tablet company
events.text: Wacom was founded to make pen tablets. Its pens sense how hard you press, using magnetic signals from the tablet, so the pen needs no battery. In 1991 it made pens without a cord.
events.why: Pressure-sensitive pens made drawing on a computer feel much more like drawing on paper.

events.title: Painting a forest you can almost smell
events.text: Oga was art director on Studio Ghibli's My Neighbor Totoro. His painted backgrounds of fields and forests gave the film its warm, living feel. In 2007 a Tokyo museum held a show about him called The Man Who Drew Totoro's Forest.
events.why: Background painting and art direction can make a place feel like a character.

events.title: Photoshop 1.0
events.text: Thomas Knoll wrote a program to show and change pictures while he was a student. His brother John, who worked at the effects studio Industrial Light & Magic, pushed him to grow it. Adobe released it as Photoshop 1.0 in February 1990.
events.why: Layers of changeable digital paint later became the everyday tool of concept artists.

events.title: Painter: paint that behaves like paint
events.who: Mark Zimmer and Tom Hedges, Fractal Design
events.text: Painter was made to copy real materials like watercolour, oils, chalk and charcoal on textured paper. With a pressure pen, its brushes respond to how you press and tilt. It is now sold by Corel.
events.why: Artists could keep their painting skills and still work digitally.

events.title: A design director for a galaxy
events.text: Lucasfilm hired Doug Chiang, born in Taipei, to lead its art department. As design director he shaped the look of the Star Wars prequels from 1999. Years later he said he designs in the iPad app Procreate.
events.why: Big films began to have whole teams of concept artists led by one design director.

events.title: Sculpting in 3D like clay
events.text: ZBrush was shown at the SIGGRAPH conference in 1999. It lets artists push and pull digital clay with brushes, with millions of tiny faces. Studios like ILM and Wētā FX use it to design creatures and props.
events.why: Designers could turn a drawing into a model you can spin and see from every side.

events.title: Illustrators draw Middle-earth
events.who: Alan Lee, John Howe and Wētā Workshop
events.text: Book illustrators Alan Lee and John Howe were the lead concept artists for Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings films. Set builders closely followed some of Lee's drawings. Lee shared the 2004 Oscar for art direction.
events.why: Concept art connected a famous book's world to the sets, props and effects built for the screen.

events.title: Villages and palaces for Hindi cinema
events.text: Desai was art director on films including Lagaan (2001) and Devdas (2002). He won four National Film Awards for art direction. In 2005 he opened ND Studios near Mumbai.
events.why: Designing a film's world on a grand scale became a celebrated craft in India too.

events.title: A studio in a tablet
events.text: Procreate, a painting app for the iPad, was released in 2011. Artists at studios like Disney Animation and Pixar now use it. A sketch can start on a train and end up in a film.
events.why: Concept art tools became portable, cheap and easy to learn.

events.title: A kingdom drawn 15,000 times
events.who: Sabu Cyril and the Baahubali team
events.text: For Baahubali: The Beginning, production designer Sabu Cyril designed a whole kingdom, including thousands of weapons and armour pieces. About 15,000 storyboard sketches were made before filming. VFX studios such as Makuta VFX in Hyderabad then built its biggest sights.
events.why: It showed Indian cinema designing fantasy worlds at the same scale as Hollywood.

events.title: A film that looks like a comic
events.who: Justin K. Thompson and Sony Pictures Animation
events.text: For Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, the team drew and painted comic-book lines, dots and textures on top of 3D frames. Production designer Justin K. Thompson helped set the style. It won the Oscar for best animated film.
events.why: Visual development can invent a brand new look for a whole kind of film.

events.title: Building 1920s India for RRR
events.text: Sabu Cyril was production designer on RRR. His team built a big village set and a copy of old Delhi at Ramoji Film City. The film became a worldwide hit, and its song Naatu Naatu won an Oscar.
events.why: Careful design of a past world helped an Indian film reach audiences everywhere.

firsts.label: "Production designer" credit
firsts.who: William Cameron Menzies, Gone with the Wind

firsts.label: Photoshop 1.0
firsts.who: Thomas and John Knoll, Adobe, USA

people.name: Albert Hurter
people.note: Disney's first inspirational sketch artist, drawing freely to spark ideas for Snow White and Pinocchio.

people.name: William Cameron Menzies
people.note: The first person credited as production designer, on Gone with the Wind.

people.name: Gustaf Tenggren
people.note: His fairy-tale paintings shaped the look of Snow White and Pinocchio.

people.name: Kay Nielsen
people.note: Painted the dark mountain of Fantasia and early Little Mermaid ideas.

people.name: Mary Blair
people.note: Brought bold modern colour to Cinderella, Alice, Peter Pan and It's a Small World.

people.name: Satyajit Ray
people.note: Planned his films in sketchbooks and red notebooks full of drawings.

people.name: Ray Harryhausen
people.note: Drew dramatic key drawings before animating his famous creatures.

people.name: Ralph McQuarrie
people.note: His 1975 paintings helped Star Wars get made.

people.name: Syd Mead
people.note: Designed the future cities and vehicles of Blade Runner and worked on Tron.

people.name: Kazuo Oga
people.note: Painted the forests and fields of My Neighbor Totoro.

people.name: Doug Chiang
people.note: Has led Star Wars design at Lucasfilm since 1995.

people.name: Sabu Cyril
people.note: Designed the worlds of Baahubali and RRR, and has won four National Film Awards.

facts: About 15,000 storyboard sketches were made for Baahubali: The Beginning before filming.
Kay Nielsen's Little Mermaid paintings from the late 1930s waited about 50 years for Disney to make the film in 1989.
The Ray and Diana Harryhausen Foundation looks after more than 50,000 items, including his drawings and models.
Photoshop 1.0 had just one engineer, Thomas Knoll, and was written mostly in the Pascal language.
Satyajit Ray had no written script for Pather Panchali at first: he planned it in drawings.
